'''Sir Henry Peter Francis Swinnerton-Dyer, 16th Baronet''', {{post-nominals|country=GBR|sep=,|KBE|FRS}} (2 August 1927 &ndash; 26 December 2018) was an English [[mathematician]] specialising in [[number theory]] at the [[University of Cambridge]]. As a mathematician he was best known for his part in the [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] relating algebraic properties of [[elliptic curve]]s to special values of [[L-function]]s, which was developed with [[Bryan Birch]] during the first half of the 1960s with the help of machine computation, and for his work on the [[Titan (1963 computer)|Titan]] operating system.<ref>{{cite news | title=Number theory expert and co-creator of the 'beautiful' Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture | newspaper=[[Daily Telegraph]] | page=31 | issue=50890 | date=1 January 2019}}</ref>

==Biography==
Swinnerton-Dyer was the son of Sir Leonard Schroeder Swinnerton Dyer, 15th [[Baronet]], and his wife Barbara, daughter of Hereward Brackenbury. He was educated at the [[Dragon School]] in Oxford, [[Eton College]] and [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], where he was supervised by [[J. E. Littlewood]], and at some time in the late 1940s achieved the position of [[Senior Wrangler]] on the [[Mathematical Tripos]] at the latter.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sir Peter is Unhorsed |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1080327/index.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121203050232/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1080327/index.htm |archive-date=3 December 2012 |access-date=6 July 2013 |publisher=[[Sports Illustrated]]}}</ref> He also spent a year abroad as a [[Commonwealth Fund]] Fellow at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="DNB">{{Cite ODNB|doi=10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.013.90000380602|title=Dyer, Sir (Henry) Peter Francis Swinnerton (1927–2018)}}</ref>

Swinnerton-Dyer was later made a fellow of Trinity, and was master of [[St Catharine's College, Cambridge|St Catharine's College]] from 1973 to 1983 and [[Chancellor (education)|vice-chancellor]] of the University of Cambridge from 1979 to 1981. In 1983 he was made an [[List of Honorary Fellows of St Catharine's College, Cambridge|honorary fellow]] of St Catharine's.

In that same year, he became chairman of the [[University Grants Committee (UK)|University Grants Committee]] and then from 1989, chief executive of its successor, the [[Universities Funding Council]].

He was elected a [[fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1967 and was made a [[Order of the British Empire|KBE]] in 1987.<ref name="DNB"/> In 1981, he was awarded an honorary degree (Doctor of Science) by the [[University of Bath]].<ref>{{cite web  |url=http://www.bath.ac.uk/ceremonies/hongrads/  |title=Honorary Graduates 1989 to present  |publisher=University of Bath  |work=bath.ac.uk  |access-date=18 February 2012  |archive-date=17 July 2010  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717061336/http://www.bath.ac.uk/ceremonies/hongrads/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1991, he received an honorary DSc degree from [[Ulster University]].<ref>[https://www.ulster.ac.uk/about/governance/secretariat/honorary-graduates Honorary graduates conferred since 1985] Ulster University</ref> In 2006, he was awarded the [[Sylvester Medal]],<ref name="Royal Society Sylvester Medal">{{cite web | title=Sylvester Medal | website=Royal Society | url=https://royalsociety.org/grants-schemes-awards/awards/sylvester-medal/ | access-date=2022-11-08}}</ref> and also the [[Pólya Prize (LMS)]].<ref name="LMS Pólya">{{cite web | last=Sheng | first=Yunhe | title=List of LMS prize winners | website=London Mathematical Society | url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/prizes/list-lms-prize-winners | access-date=2022-11-08}}</ref>

Swinnerton-Dyer was, in his younger days, an international [[Contract bridge|bridge]] player, representing the British team twice in the European Open teams championship. In 1953 at [[Helsinki]] he was partnered by Dimmie Fleming: the team came second out of fifteen teams. In 1962 he was partnered by Ken Barbour; the team came fourth out of twelve teams at [[Beirut]].<ref>Hasenson P. ''British Bridge Almanack''. 77, London. pp. 400–1</ref>

He married [[Harriet Crawford]] in 1983.<ref>{{cite news | title=Marriages | newspaper=The Times | date=26 May 1983 | page=20 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | first=Miles | last=Reid | author-link=Miles Reid | title=Sir Peter Swinnerton-Dyer obituary | newspaper=The Guardian | date=9 January 2019 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2019/jan/09/sir-peter-swinnerton-dyer-obituary | access-date=9 August 2022 }}</ref>

===Research===

[[A. O. L. Atkin|Atkin]] and Swinnerton-Dyer verified and extended<ref name="DysonPartitions">{{cite journal | last1=Atkin | first1=A. O. L. | last2=Swinnerton-Dyer | first2=P. | title=Some Properties of Partitions | journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society | volume=s3-4 | issue=1 | date=1954 | doi=10.1112/plms/s3-4.1.84 | pages=84–106 | url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/plms/s3-4.1.84 | access-date=2025-08-03| url-access=subscription }}</ref> several conjectures of [[Freeman Dyson]]<ref>{{cite journal|first=Freeman J.|last=Dyson|title=Some Guesses in The Theory of Partitions|journal=Eureka (Cambridge)|year=1944|volume=8|pages=10–15|url=https://www.archim.org.uk/eureka/archive/Eureka-8.pdf|archive-date=10 June 2020|access-date=3 August 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610100827/https://archim.org.uk/eureka/archive/Eureka-8.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> on congruences of the partition function p(n). Extensions of Dyson's musings on congruences of the partition function continue to be an active area of research.

In the late 1950s Swinnerton-Dyer began a collaboration<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Birch |first1=Bryan |author-link=Bryan John Birch |last2=Swinnerton-Dyer |first2=Peter |author-link2=Peter Swinnerton-Dyer |year=1965 |title=Notes on Elliptic Curves (II) |journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik|J. Reine Angew. Math.]] |volume=165 |issue=218 |pages=79–108 |doi=10.1515/crll.1965.218.79 |s2cid=122531425 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Coates | first1=John | last2=Birch | first2=Bryan | last3=Colliot-Thélène | first3=Jean-Louis | last4=Skorobogatov | first4=Alexei | title=Memorial Tribute: Peter Swinnerton-Dyer (1927–2018) | journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society | publisher=American Mathematical Society (AMS) | volume=66 | issue=7 | date=2019-08-01 | issn=0002-9920 | doi=10.1090/noti1920 | doi-access=free | page=1}}</ref> with [[Bryan John Birch|Bryan Birch]], exploring ideas of [[Carl Ludwig Siegel|Siegel]] and [[Tsuneo Tamagawa|Tamagawa]] in the context of elliptic curves over the rationals. They did extensive computations of elliptic curves on the Cambridge EDSAC-2, which led them to their famous [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]].

Swinnerton-Dyer<ref name="HassePrinciple">{{cite journal | last=Swinnerton-Dyer | first=H. P. F. | title=Two special cubic surfaces | journal=Mathematika | volume=9 | issue=1 | date=1962 | issn=0025-5793 | doi=10.1112/S0025579300003090 | pages=54–56 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/S0025579300003090 | access-date=2025-08-03| url-access=subscription }}</ref> was the first to construct a cubic surface over {{tmath|\Q}} for which the [[Hasse principle]] provably fails. [[Ernst S. Selmer]] had previously shown by example that the [[Hasse–Minkowski theorem]] cannot be extended to forms of degree 3.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Ernst S. Selmer | title=The Diophantine equation ''ax''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''by''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''cz''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 | journal=Acta Mathematica | volume=85 | pages=203–362 | year=1951 | doi=10.1007/BF02395746 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Atkin and Swinnerton-Dyer initiated the study of the arithmetic properties of modular forms for noncongruence subgroups in the late 1960s, and observed very interesting congruence relations for such forms. They conjectured that<ref name="UnboundedDenominators"> {{Citation | last1=Atkin | first1=A. O. L. | last2=Swinnerton-Dyer | first2=H. P. F. | title=Combinatorics (Univ. California, 1968): Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics, vol. XIX | publisher=American Mathematical Society | year=1971 | chapter=Modular forms on noncongruence subgroups | pages=1–26}}</ref> if a modular form {{math|''f''(τ)}} is not modular for some [[congruence subgroup]] of the [[modular group]], then the Fourier coefficients of {{math|''f''(τ)}} have unbounded denominators, which became known as the Atkin-Swinnerton-Dyer unbounded denominators conjecture. The conjecture was proved by [[Frank Calegari]], Vesselin Dimitrov and [[Yunqing Tang]] in 2021. <ref name="UnboundedDenominatorsProved">{{cite arXiv |eprint=2109.09040 |last1=Calegari |first1=Frank |last2=Dimitrov |first2=Vesselin |last3=Tang |first3=Yunqing |title=The Unbounded Denominators Conjecture |date=2021 |class=math.NT }}</ref>

===Death===

Swinnerton-Dyer died on 26 December 2018 at the age of 91.<ref>{{cite web|title=Professor Sir Peter Swinnerton-Dyer Bt KBE FRS (1927–2018)|date=28 December 2018|website=St. Catharine's College, Cambridge|url=https://www.caths.cam.ac.uk/about-us/news-and-events/professor-sir-peter-swinnerton-dyer-bt-kbe-frs-1927-2018}}</ref>
